hints: Focus on both conditions separately, shape from electron pairs and total covalent bonds by counting every shared pair, not just bond locations.
Start with methane, it has four bonding pairs and no lone pairs on carbon, so work out its shape and bond count first.
Now compare each pair carefully, remember a double bond counts as two covalent bonds and a triple bond counts as three.
walkthrough:
**Recall what controls shape and bond number**

Shape is decided by the number of bonding pairs and lone pairs around the central atom. Number of covalent bonds means count every shared electron pair.

Remember:
$$\text{single bond = 1 covalent bond, double bond = 2, triple bond = 3}$$

**Check methane and the ammonium ion**

Methane, $\text{CH}_4$, has 4 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs on C, so tetrahedral with 4 covalent bonds. Ammonium, $\text{NH}_4^+$, has 4 bonding pairs (one is dative) and 0 lone pairs on N, so also tetrahedral with 4 covalent bonds.

Both conditions match:
$$\text{CH}_4 \text{ : tetrahedral, 4 bonds} \quad \text{NH}_4^+ \text{ : tetrahedral, 4 bonds}$$

**Test the other pairs and conclude**

Carbon dioxide, $\text{CO}_2$, is linear with two double bonds, so 4 covalent bonds, while nitrogen, $\text{N}_2$, is linear with one triple bond, so 3 covalent bonds. Boron trifluoride, $\text{BF}_3$, is trigonal planar while ammonia, $\text{NH}_3$, is trigonal pyramidal. Water, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, is bent while oxygen, $\text{O}_2$, is linear.

Only the first pair matches on both shape and bond number.

options.A: Correct. Both $\text{CH}_4$ and $\text{NH}_4^+$ have 4 bonding pairs and no lone pairs on the central atom, so both are tetrahedral. Both have 4 single covalent bonds (the fourth N-H bond in ammonium is a dative covalent bond but still counts as one covalent bond).
options.B: Incorrect. Both $\text{CO}_2$ ($\text{O=C=O}$) and $\text{N}_2$ ($\text{N}\equiv\text{N}$) are linear, so shape matches. But bond number does not: $\text{CO}_2$ has 2 double bonds = 4 covalent bonds, while $\text{N}_2$ has 1 triple bond = 3 covalent bonds.
options.C: Incorrect. Both have 3 covalent bond locations, $\text{BF}_3$ has 3 B-F bonds and $\text{NH}_3$ has 3 N-H bonds. But shape does not match: $\text{BF}_3$ has 3 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs so trigonal planar, while $\text{NH}_3$ has 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair so trigonal pyramidal.
options.D: Incorrect. Both have 2 covalent bonds in total: $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ has 2 O-H singles, $\text{O}_2$ has 1 O=O double ($\text{O=O}$ counts as 2). But shape does not match: $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ has 2 bonding pairs plus 2 lone pairs so bent, while $\text{O}_2$ with only two atoms must be linear.
